titulo.texto: Funerary Urn of the God Cocijo

frase_gancho.texto: Cocijo, the Zapotec god of rain, a relative of Tláloc, with goggle eyes and fangs.

puente_narrativo.texto: From the god of rain we move on to the god of maize, because without one there is no other. Look for another seated urn, whose headdress has no goggle eyes or fangs, but ears of corn.

guion_corto.texto: This seated figure, made of gray clay, is Cocijo, the Zapotec god of rain, thunder and lightning. It stands almost forty centimeters tall. Look at his face: he has thick goggles around his eyes, a mask over his mouth from which curved fangs emerge, and, on his headdress, a sign that specialists call Glyph C, related to the vessel that holds the waters of the sky. His hands rest on his knees, in a solemn posture. Urns like this one did not hold the ashes of the dead: they were placed in niches and tombs, and served as guardians. For a people of farmers, asking Cocijo for water was asking him for life.

guion_largo.texto:
If the Tláloc outside the museum impressed you, here is his relative from Oaxaca. He was called Cocijo, or Pitao Cocijo, a name that is usually translated as «the great lightning», and like Tláloc he ruled over rain, thunder and clouds. The Zapotecs themselves, it is said, called themselves «people of the clouds». For them rain was no minor detail: maize depended on it, and everything depended on maize.

Look at the face. Around the eyes there are thick goggles, like the ones Tláloc wears; over the mouth, a kind of forked mask, from which curved fangs emerge that are sometimes read as a serpent's tongue. At the center of the headdress there is a sign, Glyph C, which Alfonso Caso, the archaeologist who explored Monte Albán, named with that letter. It is related to a water vessel or to lightning, and it is repeated on many urns. It is like Cocijo's seal. And it is so frequent that Caso and his colleague Ignacio Bernal published an entire catalog of these figures, called Urnas de Oaxaca: there are hundreds, and many wear the same headdress.

These figures are called urns, but the name is misleading. They did not hold the ashes or the bones of the deceased. They were placed in niches, on the facades and in the corners of tombs, and they worked as guardians and as messengers: it is thought that, through them, the ancestors interceded with the gods so that it would rain. Some had, on the back, a receptacle where copal was burned, the same incense you already saw in the braziers of Teotihuacán, so that prayers would rise with the smoke.

Notice how it was made. The body was modeled by hand, and the ornaments, such as the beaded pectoral and the headdress, were attached afterward, some made with a mold and others with little strips and balls of clay. If you get closer, you will see that the decoration was built piece by piece, like a necklace. It preserves traces of red paint, and some of Cocijo's sister urns also keep remnants of blue.

Every people had its own god of rain. The Mexica called him Tláloc; the Maya, Chaac; the Mixtecs, neighbors of the Zapotecs, Dzahui, and they called themselves «people of the rain». This is not the same god with another name, but related gods: all were born of the same need, that of having water arrive on time. In the Maya Hall you will see the face of Chaac, with a long nose that curls upward.

The bond with water was so strong that, even today, in some communities of Oaxaca ceremonies are held to ask for rain, on hills and in caves, with offerings, flowers and copal. It is a custom that surely goes back much further than Cocijo. When you go up to the ethnography halls, you may recognize that thread.

Look at his posture: seated, solemn, with his hands on his knees. He is a god in no hurry, who has nothing to prove. Behind that calm there is a restrained thunder. A clay figure, almost forty centimeters tall, that has spent more than a thousand years saying the same thing: without water, there is no maize.

texto: Look for the round goggles around the eyes
Find the headdress and the sign that crowns it
Look at the mouth: what comes out of it?

texto.Material: Modeled clay ceramic, with traces of polychrome paint or slip
texto.Origin: Monte Albán, Central Valleys, Oaxaca (another Cocijo example comes from Atzompa)
texto.Dimensions: 0.396 m high x 0.38 m wide (central urn from Tomb 104; other examples are larger)

texto.pregunta: Myth: Cocijo and Tláloc are the same god with a different name.
texto.respuesta: Reality: They are related gods: every people had its own god of rain, with its own name, face and myths. They look alike because they all answered the same need: water for the maize.
